title: Costs
text:
Costs
This section presents an order-of-magnitude framework for estimating the financial impact of customer churn at the bank using the provided historical credit card customer data.

Since the available dataset does not contain customer profitability, retention costs, or detailed financial reporting information, the true economic impact of churn cannot be measured directly. Instead, we estimate the order-of-magnitude financial impact of churn using commonly used business metrics and reasonable assumptions derived from the credit card industry.
The estimated cost of churn consists of two components

Lost Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)

this is the future value that would have been generated had a customer remained with the bank

Customer Acquisition Cost (CaC)

this is the cost of replacing a departed customer with a newly acquired customer


The total estimated order-of-magnitude financial impact of churn can therefore be approximated as
\[
\text{Cost of Churn} = \text{Lost CLV} + \text{Replacement Cost (CaC)}
\]
The methodology described in this section was used to estimate the order-of-magnitude financial impact of churn, the results of which were discussed in the previous step.
Replacement Cost or Customer Acquisition Cost (CaC)
The first component of churn cost is the expense incurred to replace a departed customer. This is commonly referred to as Customer Acquisition Cost (CaC) and includes expenditures associated with attracting, marketing to, onboarding, and servicing newly acquired customers.
Examples include

advertising and promotional campaigns
marketing and sales personnel costs
onboarding and account setup costs
technology and operational expenses associated with customer acquisition

Industry estimates suggest that customer acquisition costs for credit card products are typically in the range of approximately $167 per customer.
For the purposes of this analysis, we assume a Customer Acquisition Cost of $200 per acquired customer.
Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)
The next component of approximating the order-of-magnitude financial impact of churn is the CLV.
The two terms to estimate the CLV are total annual revenue and a tenure multiplier. The total annual revenue is the sum of all sources of credit card revenue earned by the bank per year. A CLV multiplier represents the present value of $1 of annual revenue but received over T years and discounted over time.
In the next two sub-sections, we’ll first estimate the total revenue earned by the bank and then approximate the multiplier. These two terms will then be combined to estimate the CLV.
Sources of Annual Revenue
CLV per customer is the average lifetime value retained if churned customers were convinced to stay. The bank earns fees from each customer who uses its credit card services. Each of these fees contributes to CLV. Since we don’t have access to profit per customer, we need a proxy of revenue streams for a typical credit card division within a bank using the available columns in the client’s provided churn data.
Below are the three proxies we will use for sources of annual revenue earned by the bank from providing credit card services

Revenue from Transaction activity (interchange fees)

These are fees charged based on number of credit card transactions performed by a customer. These are captured using the Total_Trans_Amt (total dollar value of all credit card transactions) and Total_Trans_Ct (total number of credit card transactions performed) columns in the provided customer churn data. Banks typically earn a fee of 1-3% of transaction volume. Here, we’ll assume this to be 2% (r = 0.02) for the client’s bank. The interchange revenue is then estimated as \[
\text{Interchange Revenue} = \text{Total\_Trans\_Amt} \times r
\tag{1}\]

Interest income from revolving balance

These are the fees captured by the Total_Revolving_Bal column in the provided customer churn data. This is the portion of the spent credit card balance (the exact amount of money spent during a billing cycle) that a customer carries over from month to month instead of paying off in full. A higher revolving balance shows that the customer actively uses credit and carries debt. Active users with higher revolving balances often show a lower likelihood of churning compared to inactive users. If a customer carries a credit card balance then it rolls over to the next month and the bank earns interest of approximately 15-20% in Canada and 20-30% in the US on this balance. Here, we will assume this to be 18% (apr = 0.18). So, the revenue earned by the client’s bank from credit card interest can be estimated using \[
\text{Interest Revenue} = \text{Total\_Revolving\_Bal} \times apr
\tag{2}\]

Premium Card Value Proxy

A credit card issuer can earn revenue beyond transaction-based revenue. One of these is an annual fee charged for holding the credit card. The customer pays this fee simply for maintaining the account, typically once per year. Annual fees are often associated with cards that provide enhanced benefits. For example, a premium card might charge an annual fee in exchange for benefits. Below are some examples of discounts offered to credit card customers

cash back

this is the percentage of money back a customer gets on purchases made using a credit card (usually 1-6%)

statement credits

these are the discounts applied to a credit card account, such as annual credits for streaming services, dining, travel, or pre-check services

retail and partner discounts

these are exclusive discounts, special sales, or enhanced reward rates (e.g. 5X points instead of 1X) that are paid for with a credit card at specific retailers, restaurants, or via bank-specific shopping portals

travel perks such as frequent flyer programs

these are discounts on travel-related expenses paid for using a credit card, such as complimentary airport lounge access, travel insurance, hotel room upgrades, or discounts on rental cars

interest free periods (or 0% APR)

this is a form of discount on financing, allowing customers to pay for large purchases over time without incurring any credit card interest charges for an introductory period

various others

concierge services, higher rewards rates, etc.



A basic credit card may have no annual fee, while a premium card may have a substantial annual card value proxy fee. The actual fee depends on the specific card product and issuer. So, if a customer has a card with a $100 annual fee, the issuer could treat that $100 as an annual revenue contribution from that customer.

Using the data available to us, we can approximate these annual fees using the Card_Category column (blue card, gold card, etc.). We’ll assume the following nominal fee structure

Blue = $0 Fees
Silver = $50
Gold = $100
Platinum = $200

We will refer to this source of revenue as Fee Revenue.

These three revenue proxies can be combined into a total estimated annual revenue per customer using
\[
\text{Annual Revenue} = \text{Interchange Revenue} + \text{Interest Revenue} + \text{Fee Revenue}
\tag{3}\]
CLV Multiplier
A CLV multiplier is a factor used to convert a customer’s annual revenue earned into an estimate of their total value over time. On its own, annual revenue gives us how much a customer generates in a single year, but customers typically stay with a business for multiple years.
So, the multiplier is needed because of two factors

First is the expected tenure of the customer. If a customer is likely to remain active for several years, then the customer’s value is the sum of annual revenue across all those years, not just one year.
Second is the time value of money. Future credit card revenues earned must be discounted because revenue received in the future is worth less than revenue received today. This adjustment reflects the time value of money, uncertainty surrounding future customer behavior, and inflation.

The multiplier accounts for this by aggregating expected future revenue into a single current value. Without it, the CLV would underestimate the customer’s true value because it would ignore the fact that annual revenue is earned repeatedly over multiple years the the customer has credit card services with the bank.






TipOpportunity Cost, Risk and Inflation





As mentioned above, the second multiplier factor captures the idea that a dollar earned today is worth more than a dollar earned in the future due to opportunity cost, risk, and inflation.
Opportunity cost means that if the bank received money today, then the bank could reinvest these earnings back into their business operations, treasury, or as capital to generate more loans and earn returns over time. Now, if instead the bank receives that money in the future, then they have missed out on those potential earnings. As a result, money received later is effectively worth less than money received today.
Risk reflects the uncertainty that future cash flows may not actually happen. A customer might cancel their credit card earlier than expected or reduce spending on the card, so future revenue is less certain.
Finally, inflation reduces purchasing power over time, so the same dollar in the future will buy less than it does today.
These three components explain why future cash flows must be adjusted downward when estimating their value today.



For these reasons, we need to use a multiplier that effectively adds up the discounted future revenues into a single factor that can be applied to the annual revenue we calculated earlier.
We will make the following simplifying assumptions to estimate the multiplier

a loyalty discount factor per year of 0.9 (d = 0.9)

this means the customer’s loyalty discount is 100%-90% = 10% per year

an expected remaining tenure per customer of 3 years (T = 3)

Estimation of CLV
We’ll now combine T, d and the estimated annual revenue to estimate the CLV per customer
\[
CLV_i = \sum_{t=0}^{T} (\text{Annual Revenue}_i \times d^t)
\tag{4}\]
The annual revenue is constant so it can be factored out as shown below
\[
CLV_i = \text{Annual Revenue}_i \times \sum_{t=0}^{T} d^t
\tag{5}\]
This can be simplified to
\[
CLV_i \approx \text{Annual Revenue}_i \times \frac{1 - d^T}{1 - d}
\tag{6}\]
This means the multiplier can be extracted as
\[
Multiplier \approx \frac{1 - d^T}{1 - d}
\tag{7}\]
We are starting immediately (t=0) instead of after one period. This is a common simplification in business settings where timing precision isn’t critical and we want a quick, interpretable multiplier.
Key Limitations
Using this CLV, we can estimate the order-of-magnitude financial impact of credit card churn at the client’s bank.
As mentioned above, the CLV estimation framework relies on several assumptions that are not directly observable in the provided dataset. These values are intended to produce a reasonable order-of-magnitude estimate of customer value rather than a precise financial valuation.

title: Credit Card Churn Modeling and Insights
text:
Welcome
Welcome to our team’s analysis of a client’s credit card customer churn data!.
Our Task
We worked with the manager of the credit card division at a full-service bank to develop a predictive model of credit card customer churn from raw customer data, in order to address the client’s issue of observed growing churn at the bank. These predictions would have to be used by the client and the client’s management team to facilitate data-driven customer retention interventions.
Throughout this project, our team used the PyData stack for scientific computing in Python, which consists of tools for performing data analysis, data visualization, statistical inference, machine learning and interactive computing.
Our Team’s Approach
In order to complete this task, we divided this project into the following five steps

Project Scoping

we used the CMU Data Science scoping guide to scope out the project
we used the provided historical customer data to quantify the impact of credit card customer churn at the bank by estimating business metrics relevant to the banking sector
we determined that our team could deliver value to the client by developing a predictive Machine Learning (ML) churn model to proactively target at-risk customers

Exploratory Data Analysis

we analysed the raw customer data using Pandas and extracted insights into and hypotheses about the bank’s credit card customer behaviour and developed hypotheses
we used these in the next step to develop predictive ML models

Machine Learning Development

based on the outputs of our data analysis, we extracted predictive ML features from the raw customer data
we trained ML models to predict customer churn, performing model validation, evaluation and inference using Scikit Learn and XGBoost with MetaFlow for orchestrating model development
we used predictions of the best ML model to estimate net savings and combined this with our model’s predicted probability of churn to segment the customers in the raw data and make targeting recommendations per customer segment

Data Validation

we developed a data model to validate the raw customer data for use in ML development
we used the Pandera data validation framework to develop the data model

Unit Testing

we wrote unit tests with the PyTest framework to test the functionality of the custom Python modules that our team developed to implement steps 1. to 4. above
we consolidated our unit tests under the tests folder on our team’s Github repository

title: Phases of Implementation
text:
Phases of Implementation
Machine Learning (ML) was used to identify customers at risk of canceling their credit card services. We used these predictions to

estimate order-of-magnitude business metrics from successfully getting these customers to revert their decision to churn with an assumed 40% success rate
make targeting recommendations by profiling customers based on one of the business metrics
understand the most important predictors that a customer would churn or be retained based on their historical behavioural attribu tes

More details, constraints and high-level assumptions are discussed later during project scoping.
We divided this task into five phases, or sections.
Project Scoping
We started by scoping the project to quantify the magnitude of the business problem facing the client. We did this with two Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) used in the finance industry to measure credit card customer churn.
After determining that the problem facing the client was important and actionable using the provided data, we performed a predictive analysis to address the client’s business problem of identifying customers at risk of churning.
To ensure all team members were working with a single source of truth, the raw customer data .xlsx file was stored in a private Cloudflare R2 bucket. All processed datasets and analysis artifacts were stored in the same bucket. Access keys were generated in order to allow team members programmatic access to the same canonical data.
Analysis
During the analysis phase, we prepared the raw data for use in a ML development workflow. We first split the raw data (../../notebooks/01_split_data.ipynb) into training, validation and test splits. We then performed exploratory data analysis (EDA) on the combined training and validation data split. During EDA (../../notebooks/03_eda_v2.ipynb), we created charts to explore the behavioural and demographic attributes of the bank’s customers in the raw data sample. We concluded this phase by developing a hypothesis about the attributes that would likely be predictors of credit customer churn at the bank.
ML Development
Next, we performed two streams of ML modeling.
Stream 1
In the first stream, we ran cost-sensitive ML experiments (../../notebooks/04_run_validation_experiments.ipynb) using subsets of the existing feature set across the same combination of training and validation data used in EDA. During this process, we identified the best combination of ML model, ML features and feature pre-processing (../../notebooks/03_get_best_validation_experiment.ipynb). We were able to validate the hypothesis developed during EDA about the choice of features that would be predictors of churn.
Next, we used a ML monitoring framework to measure concept drift and data drift during model evaluation on unseen data. i.e. the test data split, which was not seen during model validation. We found these to be negligible (../../notebooks/06_evaluate.ipynb) in the unseen data.
The best model was then trained on all available data and, per the business use-case, used to make inference predictions of all available customers data in the random sample of customer data we were provided. These predictions were used to identify the at-risk customers.
From this cohort, we used an order-of-magnitude estimate of Return on Investiment (ROI)* (../../notebooks/08_estimate_cohort_size_using_roi.ipynb) and (net) savings (../../notebooks/09_estimate_cohort_size_using_savings.ipynb) to determine the optimal cohort of at-risk customers for the client to target, for two scenarios. In scenario 1, we assumed the client’s budget allowed for a total targeting of at most 20,000 dollars. For scenario 2, we assumed that a budget of approximately 80,000 dollars was available to target all identified at-risk customers.
Stream 2
In the second stream, we developed an end-to-end ML pipeline (../../notebooks//13_production_ml_pipeline.ipynb). We demonstrated the performance of this model on the unseen (test split) data. All steps from data retrieval to ML inference were orchestrated in this pipeline. Unlike the first stream, additional features were engineered from the raw customer data. This gave an improvement in the model evaluation scores on unseen data compared to those found in the first stream.
Using the unseen data, at-risk customers were identified and model interpretability was performed. Finally, under the same conditions as scenario 2 from above, the ROI was estimated for the unseen (test split) data.
Data Validation
In order to use the ML workflow developed here with new (unseen) customer data, the new customers should have the same characteristics as those in the sample we used in this project. So, next, during the data validation phase, we developed a data model (../../notebooks/12_validate_data.ipynb) using the Pandera Python library to validate the customer data using two complimentary types of data validation tests.
Example Based Tests
First, we performed example-based data tests. A data schema was defined with with specific rules (e.g. column datatypes, constraints, etc.) and used to validate the data. These tests were focused on whether a specific input (attributes of a single customer) demonstrated the

characteristics
datatype

that we expected based on the sample data we used in ML model development in the analysis phase. These were rigid characteristics, often based on the bounds of data that were observed in the available customer data.
Hypothesis Tests
We also used hypothesis testing against a single column or combinations of columns in the raw customer data. Statistical checks were defined directly in the data validation schema. These were not rigid checks of the data. Instead, their purpose was to verify that the data followed certain statistical distributions or relationships rather than just checking individual values.
Unit Testing
During the analysis phase, we developed several custom Python modules to perform the analysis. So, in the unit testing phase, we used the Pytest Python library to write unit tests for these custom modules. The Coverage Python package was used to measure code coverage in the tests.

title: Problem Understanding
text:
Problem Understanding
This section discusses the business problem, identifies the client and quantifies the impact of the problem.
Business Problem
A full-service U.S.-based bank provides a broad range of financial products and services to its customers, including credit card products. The manager of the bank’s credit card division has observed an increasing number of customers canceling their credit card accounts and is concerned about the potential impact on customer retention, revenue, and long-term customer relationships.
To better understand this issue, the manager provided our team with a random but representative sample of historical customer data for approximately 10,100 customers observed over the preceding 12-16 months. Within this sample, approximately 16% of customers canceled their credit card services.
The manager would like to determine whether customer churn can be identified in advance using customer demographic, financial, and account usage characteristics. Specifically, the client would like to estimate which customers would have been most likely to cancel their credit card services and proactively evaluate whether targeted retention efforts could have reduced customer attrition.
Because the available dataset is historical, we will approach this task in three steps

We will begin by scoping out this project. During this process, we will assess the potential value of developing a churn modeling and targeting program by comparing performance metrics at the bank to those across the entire banking industry. If these metrics are found to place the bank at a competitive disadvantage relative to its peers then this would be an indicator that a predictive model could be valuable to the client.
If the scoping process indicates value to the client, then our team will then begin developing the predictive churn model. Customers identified by the predictive model as being at elevated risk of churn will then be treated as hypothetical candidates for retention interventions.
We will then estimate the potential business impact, costs, and benefits of offering retention incentives to these at-risk customers.

Based on this retrospective assessment using historical customer data, the client will determine whether a proactive churn management strategy should be implemented for customers who are currently active and whose future churn outcomes are not yet known.






CautionTwo Types of Customers Relevant to This Project





Historical customers are those for whom the final outcome is known, including whether they ultimately churned or remained active. These customers are captured in the provided data.
Current (or live) customers are customers who are currently active and for whom future churn outcomes are unknown. Data for these customers is not available for this project.



Business Client
Customer churn can negatively affect the bank through reduced revenue, lower customer lifetime value, increased acquisition costs required to replace the departing customers, and weakened long-term customer relationships. In order to address this, the credit card division must determine how to identify customers at elevated risk of churn and how to allocate retention resources effectively.
So, the primary business client for this project is the manager of the bank’s credit card division and the management team responsible for customer retention strategy. The management team will use the results of this project to evaluate whether predictive analytics can support a cost-effective customer retention program and improve business outcomes for both the bank and its customers.






NoteCustomers are Impacted Although they are not the Primary Client





Customers may also be negatively affected by this problem when their financial needs evolve but are not adequately addressed through competitive products, personalized services, or timely engagement. So, a successful retention strategy could improve credit card customer satisfaction by helping the bank proactively respond to changing customer needs before at-risk customers cancel their credit card accounts. However, since we only have access to historical data, bank customers are not our direct business client for this project.



Impact of Churn
how many impacted people and how much?






TipConstraints on Data Available to Make Quantitative Estimates





The client, the credit card division management team, and the bank’s customers are all affected by customer churn. However, because organizational and financial information about the bank is not available, the impact on employees and management cannot be quantified directly.



The available data contains information only at the customer level. So, the quantitative assessment of impact in this project will only focus on the effects of churn on the bank’s credit card customer portfolio.
Industry Context
Industry benchmarks suggest that customer churn remains a significant challenge across the financial services sector. Average credit card churn rates are estimated to be approximately 19% (1, 2), with some institutions experiencing high churn rates in the range of 25%-30%.
Estimated Financial Impact of Churn
Customer churn reduces the future value that customers generate for the bank. To estimate this impact, we quantified the expected value lost when a customer cancels their credit card.
Using the provided historical customer data, we estimated that each churned customer at this bank represents approximately $508 of lost Customer Lifetime Value (CLV). In addition, replacing a churned customer generally requires marketing and acquisition expenditures. Assuming a Customer Acquisition Cost (CaC) of $200 per new customer (1, 2), the estimated total loss associated with each churned customer is approximately $708.
Applying this estimate to the historical customer sample results in an estimated total churn-related loss of approximately $1.15 million. This is an order-of-magnitude estimate because it depends heavily on our CLV methodology and the assumed $200 acquisition cost.
If customer churn continues at its current level, similar losses could be incurred annually. If churn is increasing, as observed by the client, then this financial impact would be expected to grow correspondingly.
Metrics to Quantify Impact of Churn
There are two metrics for which the bank is in danger of exceeding industry standards

The historical customer sample indicates a churn rate of approximately 16%, compared with an industry benchmark of approximately 19%. While the bank currently performs somewhat better than the industry average, the client’s observed continued growth in churn could eventually reduce this advantage and result in customer attrition rates comparable to or worse than those of its competors.
Industry estimates suggest that the average credit card customer in the financial services sector generates approximately $808 of Customer Lifetime Value. Using the historical customer data, we estimated that customers who remained active generated an average CLV of approximately $877, which is above the industry benchmark. This result suggests that the bank’s current customer portfolio remains relatively valuable. However, if higher-value customers increasingly leave the bank, overall customer lifetime value could again decline toward or below industry norms.

In summary, the current churn rate and customer lifetime value estimates do not indicate that the bank is presently underperforming its peers. However, the client’s observation that customer churn is increasing suggests a potential emerging risk.
If this trend continues, the bank could experience

Increased loss of customer lifetime value
Higher customer acquisition costs required to replace lost customers
Reduced competitiveness relative to its peers
Lower long-term profitability within its credit card portfolio

For these reasons, customer churn represents a meaningful business problem that warrants further investigation and evaluation of potential retention strategies.
Reason for Prioritizing Problem Now
Addressing customer churn is a priority because the client has observed an increasing number of customers canceling their credit card services. Successfully addressing this problem could provide two important benefits

Reduce or reverse the observed increase in credit card customer churn
Improve customer satisfaction and retention by proactively identifying customers who may be considering canceling their credit card services and engaging them before they cancel their credit card accounts

As mentioned above, although the current churn rate of approximately 16% remains below the industry average of approximately 19%, continued growth in churn could cause the bank to exceed industry norms and potentially enter the higher-risk range of 25%-30% observed at some financial institutions. Acting now may allow the bank to intervene before customer attrition reaches levels that materially affect business performance.
Existing Approaches and Their Limitations
Based on the information available, the client currently lacks a systematic method for identifying which active customers are most likely to cancel their credit card services in the future. As a result, retention efforts are likely based on broad marketing campaigns, customer service interactions, managerial judgment, or customer complaints rather than data-driven estimates of churn risk. Although these approaches may help retain some customers, they do not allow the bank to prioritize its retention resources toward the credit card customers who are most likely to leave.
Without a predictive capability, the bank faces several challenges

Retention resources may be allocated inefficiently across the credit card customer base
High-risk customers may not be identified until they have already decided to leave (churned)
Marketing and customer service efforts may target many customers who were unlikely to churn
The effectiveness and return on investment of retention activities may be difficult to measure

This project seeks to address these limitations by identifying customers at elevated risk of churn and supporting more targeted retention strategies.
Other Groups or Stakeholders Involved in Scoping and Implementation
Based on common banking practices, the following additional stakeholder groups would likely be involved in the successful implementation of a churn prediction and retention program
Operational Stakeholders

Marketing team responsible for customer outreach campaigns
Customer service and call center teams responsible for direct customer engagement
Branch managers and financial advisors responsible for customer relationship management

Technical Stakeholders

Data Analytics and Data Science teams responsible for model development, monitoring, and reporting
IT department responsible for data infrastructure, deployment, security, and system integration
Data Governance and Compliance teams responsible for data privacy, regulatory compliance, and model governance

Customers

Current credit card customers who may be targeted for retention interventions based on model predictions

These stakeholders would participate at different stages of the project, including data access, model development, operational deployment, customer outreach, and ongoing performance monitoring.

title: Goals
text:
Goals
This section discusses the goals for this project.
Business Goals and Constraints
The primary objective of this project is to evaluate whether customer churn can be reduced through the use of predictive analytics and targeted retention strategies.
Because the available data is historical, the project will not directly intervene on the client’s current credit card customers. Instead, it will estimate the potential business value that could have been achieved had at-risk customers been identified and targeted before canceling their credit card services.
The project has three business goals, which we will discuss in detail next.
Goal 1 - Reduce Customer Churn
The primary goal of our project is to reduce the number of customers who cancel their credit card services by

identifying customers who show characteristics associated with future churn
evaluating whether retention interventions could have altered the future churn outcome

Goal Type: Effectiveness
Goal 2 - Improve Retention Resource Allocation
Retention activities require time, personnel, and financial resources. The project seeks to determine whether predictive analytics can help the bank prioritize retention efforts toward customers who are most likely to churn (at-risk customers) rather than distributing resources uniformly across the entire customer base.
Goal Type: Efficiency
Goal 3 - Preserve Customer Lifetime Value
Customer churn reduces future revenue and often requires additional expenses to replace lost customers. The project seeks to estimate the extent to which a targeted retention strategy could preserve customer lifetime value and reduce customer acquisition costs.
Goal Type: Effectiveness
Constraints
Below are the constraints that limit the scope of our analysis and conclusions that can be drawn from this project

The available dataset contains only historical customer records and does not include current customers.
No historical information is available regarding retention campaigns, customer outreach activities, or intervention outcomes.
The project cannot directly measure whether a retention offer would have changed a customer’s decision to cancel their credit card services.
Estimates of financial impact depend on assumptions regarding customer lifetime value, customer acquisition costs, and the effectiveness of hypothetical retention interventions. We made these estimates based on background research, but they are still estimates.
The dataset represents a sample of customers rather than the bank’s complete customer population.

As a result, our project estimates the potential value of a predictive retention program rather than directly measuring its real-world effectiveness.
Tradeoffs Across Project Goals
Most of the project’s goals are complementary. However, below are some of the tradeoffs.
Effectiveness versus Efficiency (type of Goal)
A retention strategy that attempts to contact every customer who may churn could potentially reduce more churn. However, it would also incur significantly higher costs. By comparison, a highly targeted strategy may be more efficient but it could miss some customers who cancel their credit card services.
Customer Retention versus Intervention Costs
Increasing the number or value of retention offers may improve the rate of retaining credit card customers. However, it may also increase operational and financial costs. So, the client must balance the expected value preserved from retaining the at-risk customers against the cost of implementing this intervention.
Customer Experience versus Targeting Accuracy
Aggressive outreach campaigns may improve retention among some customers but they could negatively affect customers who were unlikely to churn and do not wish to receive additional marketing offers. So, the client must balance intervention effectiveness with customer experience.
Because our project uses historical data, the impact of these three tradeoffs cannot be directly measured.

No additional internal or external datasets are available for this project, and no data linkage activities are planned.
Attributes Provided in the Data Source

Level of Granularity of the Data
The dataset is provided as tabular data at the individual customer level, with each record (row) representing a single customer. This level of granularity is appropriate for identifying individual customers who may be at elevated risk of churn.
Period of Time Covered by the Data Source
As mentioned above, in the data, customer characteristics and transaction behavior were aggregated over an observation period of approximately 12-16 months. This duration is beneficial because customer credit card usage often exhibits seasonal patterns (1, 2, 3, 4). Examples of common seasonal effects include

Increased spending during holiday periods
Reduced post-holiday spending as customers repay holiday debt
Back-to-school spending periods
Seasonal fluctuations in discretionary spending

So, a period spanning at least one full year increases the likelihood that annual spending cycles, payment behavior, and customer engagement trends are represented within the data.
Frequency of Subsequent Data Collection or Updates
The dataset contains a historical snapshot and will not be updated during the course of this project.
Because the project evaluates historical churn outcomes retrospectively, no ongoing data collection or refresh process is required.
Unique Identifiers in the Data that link it to Other Data Sources
The dataset contains a unique customer identifier (CLIENTNUM) that could potentially be used to link customer records to other internal banking systems.
No additional data sources are available for integration within the scope of this project. So, the identifier will be used only for record uniqueness and quality assurance purposes.
Owner of the Data
As mentioned in the business problem, the dataset was provided by the manager of the credit card division, who serves as the primary business stakeholder and project sponsor.
Storage Medium for the Data
The data was provided as a single Microsoft Excel (.xlsx) file.
Additional Useful Information Associated with this Data Source
The client indicated that the dataset represents a sample of the bank’s credit card customer population and was provided for the purpose of evaluating customer churn.
Ethical Issues Associated with Using this Data Source
Below are the ethical and governance considerations that apply to the use of this dataset.
Privacy and Security

Customer information will be treated as confidential.
Access will be restricted to authorized project personnel.
The data will not be publicly distributed.
The dataset will be securely deleted according to the client’s data retention policies upon project completion.

Data Quality and Bias

No known data collection issues or biases were communicated to our project team.
The possibility of sampling bias, measurement bias, historical process bias, or unobserved customer characteristics cannot be ruled out in the provided data.
The dataset reflects historical customer behavior and may not fully represent future customer populations or changing market conditions.

Additional Data Desired in an Ideal Scenario
Several additional data sources could improve the ability to understand, predict, and mitigate customer churn.
Retention Intervention History
Information regarding previous retention campaigns, customer outreach efforts, incentive offers, and their outcomes would allow the effectiveness of our team’s recommended retention strategies to be evaluated directly.
Customer Service Interactions
Detailed customer support records, complaints, satisfaction surveys, and call-center interactions could provide additional signals regarding customer dissatisfaction and their risk of churn.
Product Holdings and Banking Relationships
Information about other banking products held by customers, such as mortgages, loans, savings accounts, and investment products, could improve our team’s understanding of overall customer engagement and customer loyalty.
Time-Stamped Transaction Data
Dates and times are missing in the provided data. Access to credit card transaction histories with explicit dates would enable the analysis of behavioral trends over time and support more sophisticated temporal modeling approaches.
Longer Historical Observation Periods
Additional years of historical customer data would allow the stability of churn patterns to be evaluated across changing economic conditions and customer lifecycles. This would improve the confidence in the generalizability of the our best predictive models.

As mentioned above, we created a new binary column named is_churned based on the existing Attrition_Flag column. This converts the text labels as follows

Existing Customer is mapped to 0 (customer did not churn)
Attrited Customer is mapped to 1 (customer did churn)

This is essential because machine learning models require numerical values to perform classification tasks. Once this conversion was done, the original Attrition_Flag column is no longer needed and so it was dropped.
Split Data
Now, we will create the following data splits

training

will be used to determine the best ML model, including

decision threshold tuning using cross-validation
hyperparameter tuning, with best decision threshold, using cross-validation


validation

will be used to determine best customer segmantation using business metrics

test

will be used to evaluate

performance of best ML model using ML metrics
business metrics to be expected in production




# get train and test split

    df,
    test_size=size_val / (1 - size_val),
    random_state=88,
    shuffle=True,
    stratify=df[label],
)

# get validation split

    df_train,
    test_size=size_val / (1 - size_val),
    random_state=88,
    shuffle=True,
    stratify=df_train[label],
)

# show number of observations in each split
n_rows_total = len(df_train) + len(df_val) + len(df_test)
n_rows_cv = int(len(df_train) / n_cv_folds)
frac_rows_cv = 100 * n_rows_cv / (len(df_train) + n_rows_cv)
frac_rows_val = 100 * len(df_val) / (len(df_train) + len(df_val))
frac_rows_test = (
    100 * len(df_test) / (len(df_train) + len(df_val) + len(df_test))
)
print(
    f"Training Size: {len(df_train):,}\n"
    f"Cross-Validation Fold Size (Estimate): "
    f"{n_rows_cv:,} ({frac_rows_cv:.2f}%)\n"
    f"Validation Size: {len(df_val):,} ({frac_rows_val:.2f}%)\n"
    f"Test Size: {len(df_test):,} ({frac_rows_test:.2f}%)"
)


val_fold_diff = len(df_val) - n_rows_cv
val_fold_diff_pct = 100 * val_fold_diff / n_rows_cv
Markdown(
    f"""The sizes of the cross-validation fold (approximately {n_rows_cv:,}) validation split
    (approximately {len(df_val):,}) are reasonably clos to each other. Ideally, if the
    `test_size` is fixed across both splits (train+validation and train+test), the sizes of the
    cross-validation fold, validation split and test split would be identical. Due to the non-
    rounded size of the raw data, there are {val_fold_diff} (or ~{val_fold_diff_pct:.0f}%) fewer
    observations in the validation fold than in the test fold. We will assume this difference is
    acceptable and further fine-tuning of the split sizes will not be performed.
    """
)







CautionAccount for Class Imbalance when Splitting Data





startify=True was used to create splits due to the known class imbalance of the labels (is_churned) column in the data.



From adding up the totals, it is also reassuring that all observations from the raw data have been used in the data splits, as expected. This is verified below

assert len(df) == n_rows_total







ImportantRationale for Performing Pre-Processing Data Before Splitting





The simple pre-processing steps in the previous section could be performed without leaking data from the validation split into the train split, and similarly from the test into the combined train+validation split. There were no missing values to be imputed and no duplicates so our pre-processing workflow did not learn patterns from the data to be used in model validation or evaluation to clean the training data. For this reason, we were able to pre-process the data as we did before splitting it in this section.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
About
In this step, we will explore the combined train and validation data for patterns that will inform the validation phase of ML model development.
We will first look at the class imbalance in the dependent variable (customer churn). This will determine our approach to reliably scoring the predictions of a ML model for this business use-case.
We will then look to identify features that are strong predictors of customer churn. This will determine which features we should prioritize for use in model training, how we should pre-process the features and which family of models are likely to be better choices to predict the outcome in this dataset.






NoteOutputs



Charts will be saved in reports/figures. Nothing will be exported to the R2 bucket.

Exploratory Data Analysis
We will explore the combined training and validation data based on the type of features in three steps

Code

    .tab_style(style=style.text(weight="bold"), locations=loc.column_header())
    .tab_header(md("**Class Imbalance**"))

        locations=loc.body(columns=["outcome"]),
    )

    )

        columns=[
            "proportion",
        ],
        decimals=3,
    )

gt


Observations

The class labels show a medium class imbalance. Standard ML classifiers typically aim to maximize overall accuracy. Unfortunately, in an imbalanced context, this often results in a model that predicts the majority class for every customer. These predictions would have high accuracy, but it would have zero recall for the churned customers, making it useless for our business goal. This happens since the default decision threshold of 0.5 fails since it assumes that the costs of a False Positive (predicting a loyal customer will churn) and a False Negative (failing to identify a customer who actually churns) are equal. For customer churn, the cost of False Negatives, or the cost of losing a customer’s lifetime value and the cost of acquiring a new one, is high. Also, the cost of False Positives, the cost of a retention offer or a phone call to a customer who wasn’t planning to leave, is lower. So, the default decision threshold of 0.5 is of no use to use here. We will need to optimize this threshold.
In order to solve this problem, we need to move beyond simple accuracy and toward cost-sensitive learning. In scikit-learn in Python, one approach is to use nested cross-validation and TunedThresholdClassifierCV(). The inner cross-validation loop optimizes the decision threshold. This allows the model to become more sensitive to the (minority) churn class. By nesting this process within an outer cross-validation loop, we ensure that the performance metrics we report are not overfitted to the specific threshold found. The outer loop validates how well the entire ‘tuning process’ generalizes to unseen data.
Using .predict_proba() allows us to rank customers by churn risk, for the client. But, by determining an optimal decision threshold, we can reliably convert these soft labels into hard labels that we can use to reliably identify those customers who are truly at risk of canceling their credit card services at the bank. Customers with a predicted probability above this threshold are at risk of churning, while those below are not at risk. This approach will ensure the client’s targeting resources are allocated efficiently on those at risk of churning only.
For scikit-learn models, we can use class_weight="balanced". For XFBClassifier(), we can use scale_pos_weight to perform cost-sensitive learning.







NoteHandle Class Imbalance in XGBClassifier



For XGBClassifier(), class imbalance will be handled by estimating the optimal scale_pos_weight as the ratio of negative to positive samples, calculated as
\[
\frac{\sum \text{negatives}}{\sum \text{positives}}
\tag{1}\]


So, in order to calculate scale_pos_weight, we will first use sklearn’s compute_class_weight() to get the weights of the positive and negative classses

# utilize inverse of class distribution (class imbalance ratio)
class_weights_train = skut.class_weight.compute_class_weight(
    class_weight="balanced",
    classes=df["outcome"].squeeze().unique().to_numpy(),
    y=df["outcome"].squeeze().to_numpy(),
)
class_weights_train = {
    c: float(w) for w, c in zip(class_weights_train, [0, 1])
}
print(class_weights_train)


Next, we will divide the weight of the negative class by the weight of the positive class to get the value for scale_pos_weight

scale_pos_weight = class_weights_train[1] / class_weights_train[0]
print(scale_pos_weight)

This value should be hard-coded using XGBClassifier(scale_pos_weight=...) before training.

Feature Collinearity
Collinearity occurs when two or more predictor variables are highly correlated. This means they provide redundant information. In ML models, this can lead to unstable coefficient estimates (in linear models) or diluted feature importance (in tree-based models). When features show near-perfect correlation, keeping both makes it difficult to determine which specific variable is actually driving the prediction.
For a bank, a black box prediction is only partially useful. Explainability allows the client to 1. Understanding whether a customer is prone to churn due to low engagement (total_trans_ct) versus declining spend (total_amt_chng_q4_q1). This difference is important since it allows for the client to develop personalized retention offers. 2. In financial services, the ability to explain why a certain action (or lack thereof) was taken regarding a customer account is often a legal or internal audit requirement.
By excluding redundant, highly correlated features, we can make it easier for the model to extract clear, actionable insights using tools like SHAP or feature importance rankings.

chart


Observations

Customers with 2 or 3 dependents are the most common among the sample of credit card customers in the data we have.
Churn counts appear to scale proportionally with the size of the segment.
(Re-Grouping Rare Categories) Although this feature appears as a count, we will treat this as a categorical. The effect of dependents on churn is likely not linear. For example, the difference in lifestyle/financial need between 0 and 1 dependent might be similar to the difference between 4 and 5, or entirely different. Categorical encoding allows a model (like RandomForestClassifier() or XGBoostClassifier()) to learn specific, non-linear impacts for each specific count (e.g. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5). So, we will combine 4 and 5 into a new category 4+, which causes all sub-categories to occur with >=9% frequency in the combined train+validation data, and eliminates one which has a frequency of ~4.2%
Across all categories, the churn rate has a modest increase from ~14.7% (0 dependents) to ~ 17.7% (3 dependents). So, this too looks like a weak predictor of churn.

Education Level of Customer
Next, we will show the customer count in both groups of customers by their level of education

chart = vzu.plot_altair_bar_chart(

(Re-Grouping Rare Categories) We will combine the two lowest frequency sub-categories Post-Graduate and Doctorate into a category called Post-Graduate, as both levels of education are similar to each other and are above all other sub-categories. This causes all sub-categories to occur with >10% frequency in the combined train+validation data, and eliminates two which each have a frequency of <~5%.
Excluding the two highest categories by churn rate, which are also the two rarest caregories in this feature, the churn rate is nearly unchanged increasing from ~15.1% (College) to ~16.3% (Unknown). This too looks like a poor predictor of credit card churn.

Income Category of Customer
Finally, we will show the customer count in both groups of customers by their income level

Observations

The Less than $40K group is the largest segment and it contributes the highest absolute number of churners.
(Re-Grouping Rare Categories) We will combine 80K-120K and 120K + since these are generally high-income customers. Similar to education_level, this causes all sub-categories to occur with >10% frequency in the combined train+validation data, and eliminates one which has a frequency of <~7%.
As with other non-numerical features, churn behavior appears relatively consistent across different income brackets. This also looks like a poor predictor of customer churn in the sample credit card customer data.

Summary
As we can see, there are some categorical and ordinal features with rare categories (categories that do not occur frequently in the dataset). They result in unnecessary high-dimensional, sparse transformed features that lead to models overfitting to noise instead of learning meaningful patterns. So, we recommend to either drop or group these rare categories to improve the usefulness of the feature as described per feature above.
Handling Sensitive Features
Below are the sensitive features in the data

age
gender
marital_status
dependent_count
education_level
income_category

According to Kamiran and Calders, sensitive features can be used as predictive features. However, they must be handled through specific preprocessing techniques to avoid illegal and unethical discrimination of customers during a targeted marketing campaign (as is the overall use-case for this project) based on theses sensitive.
One recommended approach to ensure the predictive model does not unfairly discriminate based on age is to remove the sensitive feature and other features that correlate most with it, reducing the model’s reliance on potentially discriminatory information. customer_age is not strongly correlated to other features, as shown above. So, this approach will be used for customer_age. It will be excluded from ML model development.
gender is a balanced categorical feature that has two sub-categories that occur with almost the same frequency. So, we don’t need to group any sub-categories and this feature could be kept unchanged.
Based on observations above, categorical and ordinal features do not appear to be predictors of churn on their own. So, we will run ML experiments to determine if the other sensitive features (which are either categorical or ordinal) can be dropped without negatively impacting model performance.
Feature Lists by Type
Based on the EDA from above, features using in ML development should exclude the following

correlated numerical features
single-valued feature (card_category)
identifier features (clientnum)
sensitive feature (customer_age)

With this in mind, the ordinal, categorical and numerical features to be used in validation and evaluation are shown below

ordinal_features = [
    "income_category",
    "education_level",
]

categorical_features = [
    "gender",
    "marital_status",
    "dependent_count",
]

# keep
# - 'credit_limit' and exclude "avg_open_to_buy" which is correlated
# - 'total_revolv_bal' and exclude "avg_utilization_ratio" which is correlated
numeric_features_1 = [
    "months_on_book",
    "num_products",
    "months_inactive_12_mon",
    "contacts_count_12_mon",
    "total_amt_chng_q4_q1",
    "total_trans_amt",
    "total_trans_ct",
    "total_ct_chng_q4_q1",
    "credit_limit",
    "total_revolv_bal",
]

# keep
# - 'avg_open_to_buy' and exclude "credit_limit" which is correlated
# - 'avg_utilization_ratio' and exclude "total_revolv_bal" which is correlated
numeric_features_2 = [
    "months_on_book",
    "num_products",
    "months_inactive_12_mon",
    "contacts_count_12_mon",
    "total_amt_chng_q4_q1",
    "total_trans_amt",
    "total_trans_ct",
    "total_ct_chng_q4_q1",
    "avg_open_to_buy",
    "avg_utilization_ratio",
]

Below is a summary of the features to be used in ML validation experiments based on the EDA performed above


Code
gt = (
    GT(
        show_df(
            df[ordinal_features + categorical_features + numeric_features_1],
            False,
        )[0].reset_index()
    )
    .tab_header(md("**Summary of Features for Use in ML Experiments**"))
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="yellow"),
        locations=loc.body(columns=["num_missing"]),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="aliceblue"),
        locations=loc.body(columns=["num_unique"]),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="papayawhip"),
        locations=loc.body(columns=["dtype"]),
    )
    .tab_style(style=style.text(weight="bold"), locations=loc.column_header())
)
gt


Conclusion
We identified that behavioral metrics (numerical features like usage frequency, transaction amounts, and utilization) are stronger predictors than static demographics (categorical or ordinal features such as age, education, etc.). Features like total_trans_ct, total_revolv_bal, and avg_utilization_ratio show a distinct separation between classes (churn versus no churn). This makes them high-priority candidates for ML model development.
The bivariate analysis revealed that churners aren’t just “low users”; they often show a sharp velocity decline. The strong clustering in the total_ct_chng_q4_q1 vs. total_amt_chng_q4_q1 scatter plots suggests that creating additional ‘momentum’ features—such as ratios of activity over shorter time windows—could significantly improve model performance.

Based on these findings, our hypothesis is that numerical features are sufficient on their own to develop a ML model that can predict customer churn. this hypothesis should be verified during ML model validation (next notebook).
Our proposed pipeline involves using tree-based models (which are robust to the skewness observed in numerical feature distributions), cost-sensitive learning (with class_weight='balanced') and scikit-learn’s TunedThresholdClassifierCV() to optimize for recall or f2-score (which prioritizes recall).

About
In this step, we will evaluate all 24 runs across the five ML experiments performed as part of the validation analysis performed in the previous step.
So, here, we will determine the best combination of inputs to the ML pipeline: features, feature preprocessing and classifier (ML model).






NoteOutputs



None


Python Imports
The required Python modules are imported below


Code
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, loc, md, style
from metaflow import Flow


Import a custom Python module for post-processing the outputs of cross-validation

import cc_churn.tuning as tn

User Inputs
Below we define variables that will be used later in this notebook

primary_metric_val = "prauc"
threshold_overfit = 5

# columns to retrieve from experiment runs
cols_expt_compare = [
    "experiment_num",
    "run_id",
    "feat_group",
    "model_name",
    "threshold",
    "fit_time",
    "score_time",
    f"train_{primary_metric_val}",
    f"test_{primary_metric_val}",
    "train_f2",
    "test_f2",
    "pct_diff",
    "is_overfit",
    "is_overfit_significant",
]

# columns to display
columns_formatted = [
    "threshold",
    "fit_time",
    "score_time",
    f"train_{primary_metric_val}",
    f"test_{primary_metric_val}",
    "train_f2",
    "test_f2",
    "pct_diff",
]

Comparison of Validation Experiments
The results produced by the experiments to optimize feature selection and model selection are now compared.
Get a list of all Metaflow flow runs

metaflow_experiment_runs = list(Flow("ValidationFlow").runs())

Verify all runs are finished

assert all(list(map(lambda x: x.finished, metaflow_experiment_runs)))

Results from all experiments are combined and sorted in descending order of the primary evaluation metric for model validation (prauc)

cv_results_tuned_models = {
    f"{run.data.df_cv['model_name'].head(1).squeeze()}_{run.id}": (
        run.data.df_cv.assign(
            run_id=run.id,
            experiment_num=lambda df: (
                df["feat_group"].map(
                    {
                        "[numericals_1]": 1,
                        "[numericals_2]": 2,
                        "[numericals_1,ordinals]": 3,
                        "[numericals_1,ordinals,categoricals_ohe_encoding]": 4,
                        "[numericals_1,ordinals,categoricals_no_encoding]": 5,
                    }
                )
            ),
        )
    )
    for k, run in enumerate(metaflow_experiment_runs, 1)
}
df_cv_scores_outer = tn.combine_cv_scores_thresholds(cv_results_tuned_models)
df_cv_scores_all = tn.agg_cv_scores_thresholds(
    df_cv_scores_outer, primary_metric_val, threshold_overfit
)

Numericals (Two Groupings)
Results from all six runs of experiments 1 and 2, which compared the choice of two groupings of numerical features, are shown below

df_cv_scores_expts_1_2 = (
    df_cv_scores_all[cols_expt_compare]
    .query("experiment_num.isin([1,2])")
    .sort_values(by=["model_name", "experiment_num"], ignore_index=True)
)

This is shown below


Code
gt = (
    GT(df_cv_scores_expts_1_2.drop(columns=["feat_group"]))
    .tab_style(style=style.text(weight="bold"), locations=loc.column_header())
    .tab_header(
        md(
            "**Scores from Experiments to Choose Best Group of Numerical "
            "Features**"
        )
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.fill(color="teal"), style.text(color="white")],
        locations=loc.body(columns=["model_name"]),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="yellow"),

            style.fill(color="red"),
            style.text(color="white", weight="bold"),
        ],
        locations=loc.body(columns=["is_overfit_significant"]),

gt








Caution



Model performance is assessed using the primary scoring metric for model validation discussed in the project scope and in the previous step (ML experiment configuration), namely prauc. Here, we are using this metric calculated on the data that was not used in model training for each nested cross-validation fold, so the column with the score to consider is test_prauc.


Observations

The first grouping of numerical features outperforms the second grouping for the tree-based models, but not for the linear models. However, the linear models underperform the tree-based models. For all models, the model training time was nearly unchanged across both feature groupings.
The two best performing classifiers were XGBClassifier and HistGradientBoostingClassifier for the first feature grouping.
Overfitting with XGBClassifier was significant (>5%) and nearly double that with HistGradientBoostingClassifier (~7% - 9.5% compared to 4.8% - 5.9%). For the first feature grouping, overfitting with HistGradientBoostingClassifier ws not significant (<5%).

Numericals, Numericals+Ordinals, Numericals+Ordinals+OHE Categoricals
Results from all runs of the following experiments are shown below

experiment 1 - only using numerical features
experiment 3 - using numerical and ordinal features
experiment 4 - using all features, including categoricals with one-hot encoding


df_cv_scores_expts_1_3_4 = (
    df_cv_scores_all[cols_expt_compare]
    .query("experiment_num.isin([1,3,4])")
    .sort_values(by=["model_name", "experiment_num"], ignore_index=True)
)

This is shown below


Code
gt = (
    GT(df_cv_scores_expts_1_3_4.drop(columns=["feat_group"]))
    .tab_style(style=style.text(weight="bold"), locations=loc.column_header())
    .tab_header(
        md(
            "**Scores from Experiments to Test Hypothesis that Ordinal (3) and "
            "Categorical (4) Features are not Predictive of Churn**"
        )
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.fill(color="teal"), style.text(color="white")],
        locations=loc.body(columns=["model_name"]),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="yellow"),
        locations=loc.body(columns=[f"test_{primary_metric_val}"]),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[
            style.fill(color="red"),
            style.text(color="white", weight="bold"),
        ],
        locations=loc.body(columns=["is_overfit_significant"]),
    )
    .fmt_number(columns=columns_formatted, decimals=3)
)
gt


Observations

For XGBClassifier, RandomForestClassifier, LogisticRegression_imbalanced, Ensemble__VotingClassifier and LogisticRegression, performance with the ordinal and categorical features was nearly unchanged.
The increase the training time (see fit_time) from the inclusion of these two groups of features was also nearly unchanged.
 For each expeiment run, the Ensemble__VotingClassifier has a lower score than one of the two best performing tree-based classifiers used in the same run (XGBClassifier or HistGradientBoostingClassifier) since it also included weaker models such as LogisticRegression and RandomForestClassifier.
Among the two best models, overfitting with XGBClassifier was again significant (>5%) and higher that with the HistGradientBoostingClassifier model.

Numericals, Numericals+Ordinals, Numericals+Ordinals+Unencoded Categoricals
Results from all runs of the following experiments are shown below

experiment 1 - only using numerical features
experiment 3 - using numerical and ordinal features
experiment 5 - using all features, including categoricals with categorical encoding performed by the classifier


df_cv_scores_expts_1_3_5 = (
    df_cv_scores_all[cols_expt_compare]
    .query("experiment_num.isin([1,3,5])")
    .query("model_name == 'HistGradientBoostingClassifier'")
    .sort_values(by=["model_name", "experiment_num"], ignore_index=True)
)

This is shown below


Code
gt = (
    GT(df_cv_scores_expts_1_3_5.drop(columns=["feat_group"]))
    .tab_style(style=style.text(weight="bold"), locations=loc.column_header())
    .tab_header(
        md(
            "**Scores from Experiments to Compare Numerical (1), Ordinal (3) and "
            "Unencoded Categorical (5) Features**"
        )
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.fill(color="teal"), style.text(color="white")],
        locations=loc.body(columns=["model_name"]),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="yellow"),
        locations=loc.body(columns=[f"test_{primary_metric_val}"]),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[
            style.fill(color="red"),
            style.text(color="white", weight="bold"),
        ],
        locations=loc.body(columns=["is_overfit_significant"]),
    )
    .fmt_number(columns=columns_formatted, decimals=3)
)
gt


Observations

The inclusion of ordinal and/or unencoded categorical features (experiments 3 and 5) did not improve pipeline performance (test_prauc) relative to performance using numerical features only (experiment 1).

General Observations

In all experiments in which linear models were included, tree-based models doubled the performance of the linear models.
In all the experiments in which it was used, HistGradientBoostingClassifier and XGBClassifier had nearly identical performance (test_prauc). XGBClassifier had the shorter training time (fit_time). Both outperformed Ensemble__VotingClassifier, and strongly outperformed RandomForestClassifier. The added disadvantage of Ensemble__VotingClassifier is that its training times take an order of magnitude longer than other two.
In all experiments with top-performing tree-based models (Ensemble__VotingClassifier, XGBClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier), overfitting (in the pct_diff column) falls in the 5-10% range. XGBClassifier consistently had higher overfitting than HistGradientBoostingClassifier. For linear models and RandomForestClassifier, overfitting is less than 1% but comes at the expense of underperformance.
As seen from comparing experiments 1 or 2 (which did not include sensitive features) to 3, 4 or 5 (which did include sensitive features), model performance was not negatively impacted if sensitive features were excluded. This verifies the hypothesis we formed in the EDA step that only numerical features are sufficient to predict credit card customer churn in the sample of customer data used for this project.

Main Findings






Important



Based on the combination of the primary evaluation metric, training time and overfitting across all runs of the five experiments, the best combination of pipeline steps (features, pre-processor and ML classifier) is to use only the first grouping of numerical features that are min-max scaled (in experiment 1) and the HistGradientBoostingClassifier classifier model.








Caution



All sensitive features can be excluded from the training data without negatively impacting model performance on customer data in this dataset. This eliminates the possibliity of discrimination related to these attributes.


Get Metadata for Best Experiment
Based on the mean outer CV scores, get the best

experiment run (run_id)
experiment number
classifier name
average decision threshold

for HistGradientBoostingClassifier

# get best experiment run
df_cv_scores_best = df_cv_scores_all.query(
    "(experiment_num == 1) & (model_name == 'HistGradientBoostingClassifier')"
).nlargest(1, [f"test_{primary_metric_val}"])

# get best Metaflow run ID
best_experiment_run_id = df_cv_scores_best["run_id"].squeeze()

# get best experiment number
best_experiment_num = df_cv_scores_best["experiment_num"].squeeze()

# get best classifier
best_model_name = df_cv_scores_best["model_name"].squeeze()

# get best decision threshold
best_estimator_threshold = df_cv_scores_best["threshold"].squeeze()
# print(best_experiment_run_id)

Estimate of Model Reliability
The standard deviation of the prediction scores across outer CV folds indicates a model’s stability within each experiment. A high standard deviation suggests the model is sensitive to specific training data subsets, potentially indicating high variance or overfitting.
We will estimate model reliability from the outer CV scores during model validation by calculating the coefficient of variation (COV), which is the ratio of standard deviation to the mean, of the primary validation metric for all experiment runs

df_cov = (
    pd.concat(
        [
            # get mean and standard deviation of train and test fold scores
            (
                df_cv.groupby(
                    ["feat_group", "experiment_num", "run_id", "model_name"]
                )
                .agg(
                    {
                        f"train_{primary_metric_val}": ["mean", "std"],
                        f"test_{primary_metric_val}": ["mean", "std"],
                    }
                )
                .set_axis(
                    [
                        f"train_mean_{primary_metric_val}",
                        f"train_std_{primary_metric_val}",
                        f"test_mean_{primary_metric_val}",
                        f"test_std_{primary_metric_val}",
                    ],
                    axis=1,
                )
                .reset_index()
            )
            # iterate over all CV folds for all experiment runs
            for k, df_cv in cv_results_tuned_models.items()
        ]
    )
    # sort by experiment number
    .sort_values(by=["experiment_num"], ascending=True, ignore_index=True)
    # calculate train COV and test fold COV
    .assign(
        train_cov=lambda df: (
            df[f"train_std_{primary_metric_val}"]
            .div(df[f"train_mean_{primary_metric_val}"])
            .mul(100)
        ),
        test_cov=lambda df: (
            df[f"test_std_{primary_metric_val}"]
            .div(df[f"test_mean_{primary_metric_val}"])
            .mul(100)
        ),
    )
)

This is shown below


Code
gt = (
    GT(df_cov.drop(columns=["feat_group"]))
    .tab_style(style=style.text(weight="bold"), locations=loc.column_header())
    .tab_header(
        md(
            f"**Coefficient of Variation of {primary_metric_val} in Train and "
            "Test Fold Scores Across All CV Folds**"
        )
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.fill(color="teal"), style.text(color="white")],
        locations=loc.body(columns=["model_name"]),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="yellow"),
        locations=loc.body(columns=["run_id"]),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[
            style.fill(color="red"),
            style.text(color="white", weight="bold"),
        ],
        locations=loc.body(columns=["train_cov", "test_cov"]),
    )
    .fmt_number(
        columns=[
            f"train_mean_{primary_metric_val}",
            f"train_std_{primary_metric_val}",
            f"test_mean_{primary_metric_val}",
            f"test_std_{primary_metric_val}",
            "train_cov",
            "test_cov",
        ],
        decimals=3,
    )
)
gt


Observations

Across all outer CV folds for all classifiers (models) and across all experiment runs, the COV of the primary validation metric (prauc) is at most 5.2% on the validation split of each CV fold. This is higher than the COV of the training split per CV fold of at most 3.6%. This is partially explained by the relatively smaller size of the validation fold (~80:20 split per CV fold). For most runs, the COV is lower for the training split than for the validation split.
For the best classifier (HistGradientBoostingClassifier), the test COV is lower, falling between 1.3%-3.4%. It is reassuring that the COVs are relatively small for this ML model.
For XGBClassifier, adding ordinal (3) or catgegorical (4) features results in a higher COV on the test split than on the train split. For HistGradientBoostingClassifier, adding unencoded categorical features (5) reduces the test COV to less than the train COV.

This suggests the larger COV on unseen (validation) data is primarily due to its relatively smaller size or choice of features and/or classifier and that this does not indicate an underlying difference in the unseen data relative to the training data.
Limitations

Hyperparameter optimization was not performed.
Not all models (classifiers) that support un-encoded categorical features were compared (eg. XGBClassifier).
Ensembles contain weak and strong classifiers. Future work should exclude the weak learners.
Right-skewed histograms of numerical features during EDA suggest linear models would benefit from log-scaling. Future work should explore the addition of a pre-procesing step that includes log scaling for these models.

Conclusion
The inclusion of ordinal or categorical features made a negligible impact on model performance using prauc. This validates the hypothesis we formed during EDA that numerical features were sufficient to predict credit card customer churn.
Tree-based models have outperformed linear models. In the EDA notebook, we saw the need for using tree-based models from the skewed disributions of the numerical features that were used in model training. This finding about the relative outperformance by tree-based models when using this data verifies that observation.
In both types of models, overfitting is present but negligible.
Based on model performance, training time and overfitting, the validation analysis here indicates

the best features are numerical features only
features should be preprocessed using scikit-learn’s MinMaxScaler()
the best model (classifier) is scikit-learn’s HistGradientBoostingClassifier

title: Inference

About
In this step, the best end-to-end ML pipeline that was trained on all available data at the end of the evaluation phase is used to make inference predictions.
Inference is usually performed on data not used during ML model development. However, as discussed in the project scope, for this use-case, the final business metrics will be estimated on the all existing customer data used to develop the best end-to-end pipeline. For this reason, the inference predictions made in this step will be over the same credit card customer data used to train the best ML pipeline.

all available data and these predictions and probabilities are exported to a .parquet.gzip file. These predictions will be used in the next step to calculate business metrics on all existing customers who have churned.

all available data

User Inputs

r2_key_train = f"{prefix}/train_data.parquet.gzip"

        {

We’ll now get the best experiment ID (from evaluation) and model name (from validation)
